authority.academic_role: Prompt-time reasoning and language guidance only; never runtime facts.
authority.production_authority: Deterministic Water evidence supplied by AI Macro remains the exclusive factual record for each generation.
authority.admission_rule: Every admitted source passed the current-JIF binary gate and a complete substantive-text audit. Seven prior audits are explicitly transferred; eight sources were newly audited for Water.

foundation_result.next_gate: Independent facility, cooling, and disclosure saturation challenge WTR-CH1-016 through WTR-CH1-020

verified_admissions.title: Data centre water consumption
verified_admissions.water_extraction: Separates direct cooling water from electricity-source water; distinguishes withdrawal from consumption; defines site WUE and source-inclusive WUE; treats sparse, inconsistent operator disclosure as a measurement limitation.
limits: No universal facility intensity follows from heterogeneous cooling, climate, source and grid conditions.
WUE is denominator-sensitive and incomplete when used without source-energy water.
Secondary synthesis supports accounting language, not facility-specific causal claims.

verified_admissions.title: Using life cycle assessment to drive innovation for sustainable cool clouds
verified_admissions.water_extraction: Uses cradle-to-grave functional units to compare air, cold-plate and immersion cooling; shows that water savings can coexist with energy, refrigerant, material, spill, safety and end-of-life tradeoffs.
limits: Comparative savings are conditional on engineering and lifecycle assumptions.
Inventory proxies and missing uncertainty distributions constrain precision.
No cooling technology is universally superior.

verified_admissions.title: The environmental footprint of data centers in the United States

journal_gate.verification: Current metric crosschecked; publisher metrics page crawler-inaccessible.

whole_text_audit.format: complete IOP CC BY full text

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Links facilities, grids, utilities and watersheds to distinguish direct water, electricity-related water and scarcity-weighted impact; demonstrates that favorable national siting averages do not establish local infrastructure headroom.
limits: Facility energy and direct water are modeled, not metered comprehensively.
Annual grid attribution cannot resolve marginal or hourly supply.
A uniform cooling-water factor suppresses facility heterogeneity.

verified_admissions.title: Environmental footprints of the data center service sector in Sweden

whole_text_audit.format: complete PubMed Central JATS full text

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Shows how mixed public evidence and imputation can produce a useful inventory while leaving modeled electricity and water totals distinct from a metered census; exposes mixed-scale proxy problems in siting scores.
limits: Uniform water factors erase cooling differences.
Suitability scores are not realized performance.
Municipal or county context does not prove facility connection or supply.

verified_admissions.title: The relationship between data centers and the climate is a systems challenge: a spatial analysis of United States data centers

journal_gate.verification: Current JIF crosschecked; publisher metrics page crawler-inaccessible.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Treats water stress, heat and grid emissions as distinct spatial layers whose burdens may not align; supports exposure-screen language while rejecting conversion of ordinal risk categories into site probabilities.
limits: The location registry lacks capacity, operating state and cooling design.
Water, heat and grid measures have different periods and spatial units.
Spatial association is not facility-level causation or service availability.

verified_admissions.title: Environmental impact and net-zero pathways for sustainable artificial intelligence servers in the USA
verified_admissions.water_extraction: Separates facility and grid water in a state-level scenario model; shows that efficiency, siting and grid decarbonization have different water effects and that carbon optimization can increase hydrologic burden.
limits: Scenario ranges are conditional outputs, not forecasts with known probabilities.
Cooling configurations and future geographic allocation are modeled.
Corporate instruments are not direct physical water reductions.

verified_admissions.title: Global data center expansion and human health: A call for empirical research
verified_admissions.water_extraction: Defines plausible community and public-health pathways but makes clear that withdrawal examples alone do not establish exposure, disease incidence or facility causation.
limits: It is a research agenda, not original epidemiology.
Cited values have different denominators.
Health claims require a population, exposure, counterfactual and outcome design.

verified_admissions.title: Indicator metrics and temporal aggregations introduce ambiguities in water scarcity estimates

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete framing, seven indicators, eleven environmental-flow requirements, spatial and temporal aggregation methods, results, discussion, limitations, data and disclosures reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Using one model and common inputs, estimates change materially with indicator, environmental-flow requirement, grid versus basin aggregation, and annual versus monthly treatment. Scarcity is therefore a constructed measurement result, not a context-free site fact.
limits: Global hydrologic-model outputs do not resolve utility or facility deliverability.
Monthly, annual, basin and grid estimates answer different questions.
A single scarcity method can conceal disagreement and seasonality.

verified_admissions.title: Future global urban water scarcity and potential solutions

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete scenarios, city-demand and availability methods, solution screens, results, discussion, uncertainty, limitations, data and disclosures reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Potential supply responses—efficiency, desalination, groundwater, reservoirs, transfers and virtual-water trade—are geographically and economically conditional and can carry large investment, environmental and social consequences.
limits: Modeled feasibility is not a funded, permitted or operating project.
Scenario and input uncertainty is substantial.
A broad city-level option does not establish a campus contract or utility headroom.

verified_admissions.title: Hotspots for social and ecological impacts from freshwater stress and storage loss

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete stress, storage, vulnerability, ecological-sensitivity and adaptive-capacity construction; results; discussion; reductionist-proxy limits; methods; data and disclosures reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Freshwater stress, storage loss, exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity are separate constructs. Basin hotspot status indicates potential vulnerability and prioritization need, not a deterministic local impact.
limits: Basin totals are upper-bound exposure contexts, not universal effects.
Adaptive capacity and ecological sensitivity are proxy constructs.
Global basin analysis cannot establish facility-level availability or harm.

verified_admissions.title: Guiding urban water management towards 1.5 °C

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete perspective, scenario synthesis, supply-to-end-use boundaries, conservation, decentralized systems, river-basin allocation, sequencing, equity and research limitations reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Water-system changes must be assessed from supply through end use and over infrastructure lifecycles; end-use conservation, decentralization and basin allocation can shift energy, emissions, cost and equity outcomes.
limits: Perspective scenarios do not prove realized project performance.
Static marginal rankings can miss sequencing and cross-sector effects.
Carbon-aware water management can create affordability burdens.

verified_admissions.title: Decision making for implementing non-traditional water sources: a review of challenges and potential solutions

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete review of source definitions, quantity, quality, health, energy, cost, governance, implementation models, local externalities, research gaps and disclosures reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Rain, condensate, stormwater, recycled wastewater, greywater and desalinated water differ in quality, reliability, treatment, energy, cost, governance and infrastructure. Reclaimed-water labels alone do not establish suitability or availability.
limits: There is no one-size-fits-all alternative source.
Model comparisons must retain local permitting, financing, health and externality conditions.
Potential volume is not delivered fit-for-purpose supply.

verified_admissions.title: Pathways to a net-zero-carbon water sector through energy-extracting wastewater technologies

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete review of wastewater-energy pathways, readiness levels, membrane and catalyst constraints, methane and leakage, resource recovery, scale-up, conclusions and disclosures.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Wastewater can contain recoverable energy, water and nutrients, but recovery technologies occupy different readiness stages and introduce membrane, catalyst, leakage, chemical, energy and operating constraints.
limits: Embedded theoretical energy is not recoverable net energy.
Many pathways remain low-readiness or cost-constrained.
Recovery and reuse must account for methane leakage, water quality and additional process burdens.

verified_admissions.title: Water use in the United States energy system: A national assessment and unit process inventory of water consumption and withdrawals

whole_text_audit.extent: Complete system boundary, 17 fuel-cycle methods, source and quality classifications, withdrawal/consumption/return-flow definitions, results, data hierarchy, assumptions, limitations and supporting-information structure reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Mass-transfer definitions separate withdrawal, return flow and consumption across fuel cycles, water sources and qualities; inconsistent definitions, incomplete metering and ambiguous units are major barriers to energy-water comparison.
limits: The inventory is a 2014 national system estimate, not current plant or campus evidence.
Embodied water, foreign flows and water-quality impacts are excluded.
Data confidence varies by fuel cycle and reporting regime.

verified_admissions.title: Using water and wastewater decentralization to enhance the resilience and sustainability of cities

whole_text_audit.format: publisher full HTML plus supplementary-method register
whole_text_audit.extent: Complete unit-process model, source separation, centralized/decentralized boundary, water-energy-nutrient flows, technical/economic/environmental outputs, feasibility limits, quality constraints, conclusion and disclosures reviewed.

verified_admissions.water_extraction: Decentralized source separation can enable fit-for-purpose reuse and local resource recovery, but comparison requires functional equivalence, treatment-quality constraints, network costs, operating capability and local institutional fit.
limits: A modeled representative block is not evidence for every city or campus.
Centralized and decentralized systems cannot be compared without common service functions.
Reuse potential requires treatment, storage, distribution, monitoring and acceptance.

verified_atomic_observations.statement: Withdrawal and consumption are different physical quantities and must not be used interchangeably.
A facility water account can include direct cooling water and indirect electricity-generation water.
WUE and source-inclusive WUE use different numerators and answer different questions.
Sparse operator disclosure prevents confident facility-to-facility comparison.
Cooling choices shift burdens among water, electricity, materials, fluids, reliability and end of life.
Cooling comparisons require a common functional unit and lifecycle boundary.
Modeled percentage improvements remain conditional on engineering assumptions.
Lower operational water does not by itself establish lower total environmental burden.
Grid water can materially exceed direct site cooling water within an operational footprint.
Ordinary water volume and scarcity-weighted water impact are distinct metrics.
Watershed and grid geography determine the meaning of a national footprint estimate.
Siting scenarios are counterfactual models, not delivered infrastructure outcomes.
A heterogeneous public registry can support screening while remaining incomplete and imputation-heavy.
Uniform water factors suppress facility cooling heterogeneity.
A favorable municipal proxy does not prove a compatible utility connection or water source.
Composite suitability scores preserve their meaning only with criteria, weights and spatial scales attached.
Water stress, heat and grid emissions can be spatially misaligned.
Ordinal exposure categories are not outage or harm probabilities.
A data-center map without capacity, status and cooling design cannot establish water demand.
Mixed temporal and spatial units constrain compound-risk claims.
Facility and electricity water respond differently to siting, efficiency and grid change.
Carbon-minimizing electricity choices can increase water burden.
Future server and footprint ranges are scenario outputs rather than probability-weighted forecasts.
Certificates, offsets and restoration claims are not direct physical reductions at the site.
Water withdrawal creates a potential exposure pathway but not a demonstrated health outcome.
Cited water values with unlike denominators cannot be combined.
A research agenda must not be narrated as empirical causal evidence.
Community-impact claims require exposure, population, counterfactual and outcome evidence.
Annual aggregation can conceal seasonal scarcity visible at monthly resolution.
Scarcity estimates depend on indicator choice and environmental-flow treatment.
Grid and basin aggregation can produce materially different exposed-population estimates.
Modeled scarcity context does not establish utility deliverability to a facility.
Desalination, groundwater, reservoirs and transfers require different geography and infrastructure.
Supply expansion can impose environmental and socioeconomic consequences outside the beneficiary site.
A modeled feasible option is not a funded, permitted or operating project.
City-level supply options do not establish campus contracts or utility headroom.
Freshwater stress and freshwater storage loss are non-equivalent basin conditions.
Exposure becomes vulnerability only when combined with sensitivity and adaptive capacity.
Hotspot totals indicate potential exposure and can be upper bounds rather than realized impacts.
Basin vulnerability is not proof of a facility shortage, price event or permit constraint.
Urban water analysis should cover supply through end use over infrastructure lifecycles.
Water conservation and decentralization can shift energy, emissions and material burdens.
Static marginal rankings can miss project sequencing and cross-sector reallocation.
Water and carbon policies can create affordability and distributional burdens.
Alternative sources differ in quality, reliability, treatment, energy, cost and governance.
Potential reclaimed or harvested volume is not delivered fit-for-purpose supply.
Local permitting, financing, health and externalities condition source adoption.
There is no universally suitable non-traditional water source.
Wastewater recovery technologies shift burdens through membranes, catalysts, chemicals, leakage and energy.
Theoretical embedded energy differs from practically recoverable net energy.
Technology readiness and scale-up constraints separate laboratory potential from operating supply.
Resource recovery does not automatically equal net water, carbon or energy improvement.
Withdrawal is removal from a proximate source; consumption is the share not returned to that source.
Discharge and return flow are not identical because water can be returned to a different source.
Energy-water inventories need aligned fuel-cycle, source, quality, geography and year boundaries.
Incomplete metering and inconsistent definitions can dominate national energy-water uncertainty.
Source separation can improve fit-for-purpose reuse and resource recovery at an intermediate scale.
Centralized and decentralized systems require common service functions for fair comparison.
Reuse requires treatment, storage, distribution, monitoring and operating capability.
A representative block model does not establish feasibility for every city or campus.
